title_original: Maputo Fast Forward Marks a Decade by Questioning the Realities We Create

blocks.text: As Maputo Fast Forward celebrates its tenth anniversary, Artificial Realities: The Infinite Mirror brings Mozambique’s artistic and intellectual communities into a wider debate about artificial intelligence, cultural knowledge and creative expression. This opening frames the festival’s wider stakes before the discussion turns to Maputo itself.

In Maputo, the future of technology is being examined through the experiences, histories and creative practices of those too often excluded from defining it. As artificial intelligence reshapes how people create, communicate and interpret the world, Mozambique’s capital becomes the setting for a clear central question: what kind of society is this technology helping to create? Celebrating its tenth anniversary, Maputo Fast Forward (MFF) brings African knowledge, artistic imagination and critical thought to the centre of that conversation. A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.caption: A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.text: Taking place from 23 October to 1 November 2026 at JFS Tower in downtown Maputo, the festival unfolds under the theme Artificial Realities: The Infinite Mirror . Its central metaphor suggests a world in which images, information and identities are repeatedly reproduced, altered and reflected to us. From there, the programme examines authenticity, authorship and the relationship between human imagination and the systems that increasingly mediate it.

For Mozambique, these concerns extend beyond access to new technologies. They touch on cultural agency, the preservation of knowledge and the possibility of developing approaches to innovation informed by local experience. Rather than positioning Africa as a recipient of global developments, MFF foregrounds the continent’s capacity to define its own ideas, creative practices and critical perspectives. A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.caption: A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.text: Established by 16Neto, the festival has spent a decade connecting art, innovation and critical thinking. Its anniversary edition transforms several floors of JFS Tower into spaces for exhibitions, public discussions, performances and experimentation, bringing together artists, researchers, students and audiences from different disciplines.

The exhibitions provide a particularly compelling entry point into the festival’s concerns. Russel Hlongwane’s Ifu Elimnyama / Dzata , Dilayla Romeo’s Aerial Cartographies: Territories in Dissolution and Zayaan Khan’s Plating the Polycrisis introduce perspectives on cultural inheritance, territory and the interconnected crises shaping contemporary life. From this foundation, the exhibition space broadens the conversation beyond artificial intelligence to consider how people understand their environments and the knowledge systems that shape these relationships. A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.caption: A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.text: Nigerian artist Malik Afegbua’s Rememory, Legacy Link brings questions of memory and representation into sharper focus. Known for his work with artificial intelligence and African visual identities, Afegbua’s practice raises questions about the relationship between historical imagination and contemporary image-making. His inclusion is especially relevant at a moment when digitally generated representations of African people and histories circulate more easily, creating opportunities for reinterpretation while demanding greater attention to cultural context.

Adilson Da Oliveira’s Broadcasts for the Blind adds another dimension to the exhibitions, raising questions about perception, communication and how information is encountered. Together, these presentations demonstrate the breadth of artistic approaches within a festival that resists defining innovation exclusively through digital production, moving naturally toward the wider programme. Video Still from ‘ CHURCH OF THE HOLY PROMPT ‘ 2026. Adilson De Oliveria, Image courtesy of the artist.

blocks.caption: Video Still from ‘ CHURCH OF THE HOLY PROMPT ‘ 2026. Adilson De Oliveria, Image courtesy of the artist.

blocks.text: The conference programme extends these conversations into the social and political sphere. Philosopher Severino Ngoenha and writer Wakanyi Hoffman are among those considering ethics and humanity in the age of algorithms. At the same time, discussions involving Fátima Mimbire, Dércio Tsandzana and other participants examine environmental responsibility, democracy and the circulation of information. Artists and cultural practitioners, including Tegan Bristow and Russel Hlongwane, offer perspectives on changing conditions of artistic creation.

Beyond the formal conferences, the Rodas de Saberes (Knowledge Circles) encourage more intimate exchanges around education, gender, creative practice and African futures. Workshops led by Benjamin Gaulon explore technological repair and reuse, drawing attention to the material life of objects that are often discarded as obsolete. This practical emphasis offers another angle on progress, one that values adaptation, resourcefulness and the possibilities already present in existing materials.

Performance and film further expand the festival’s cultural reach. Nuro Sumalgy’s Raízes Digitais: Inteligência Ancestral (Digital Roots: Ancestral Intelligence) and Shaazia Adam’s The Infinite Garment (O Tecido Infinito) bring different artistic languages into the programme, while cinema, music, gaming and activities for younger audiences create chances to participate beyond established artistic and academic circles. A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.caption: A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.text: The festival’s interdisciplinary character is significant. By bringing together artistic practices concerned with cultural inheritance, ecological relationships and contemporary forms of communication, MFF shows that the questions raised by artificial intelligence cannot be separated from wider social experience. Its exhibitions and discussions argue that innovation is as much about rethinking existing relationships as it is about producing something new.

Maputo itself provides an important context for these exchanges. As Mozambique’s capital and a centre of artistic and intellectual activity, the city offers a setting where local experiences can inform conversations that often privilege perspectives from Europe and North America. In that context, the festival’s commitment to bringing together Mozambican and international participants creates opportunities for exchange without requiring African cultural practices to be understood solely through external frameworks.

The festival’s emphasis on public participation is also significant. By combining exhibitions and conferences with workshops, performances and informal encounters, MFF gives audiences opportunities to engage with complex ideas through different forms of experience. The relationship between art and technology becomes less an abstract debate and more an invitation to explore, question, and participate. A scene from a previous edition of Maputo Fast Forward. Image courtesy of Maputo Fast Forward.

blocks.text: Ten years after its establishment, Maputo Fast Forward has developed into a platform for examining the relationship between cultural expression and contemporary change. Artificial Realities: The Infinite Mirror reflects that ambition by bringing together different generations, disciplines and perspectives at a moment when the boundaries between human creativity and artificial production are being reconsidered.
From Maputo, the festival reminds us that the future is not a single vision waiting to be realised, but something continually shaped by the people, places, and histories involved in imagining it.

Maputo Fast Forward Festival 2026 takes place from 23 October to 1 November at JFS Tower, downtown Maputo, Mozambique. Admission is free. You can find more information and the full programme at www.maputofastforward.com .
